query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of interstitial carbon (on the order of 0.5 atomic percent) into the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will improve room-temperature compressive ductility without reducing its high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC solid solution known to yield 1719 MPa in compressive testing at room temperature but exhibiting low plasticity due to a high Mo content that increases the overall electronegativity difference.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 0.5 at% carbon during alloy processing (e.g., via controlled arc melting and homogenization) to introduce interstitial C atoms into the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Samples are to be synthesized under identical processing conditions, then subjected to room-temperature compression tests. Microstructural characterization (e.g., using TEM/SEM) should confirm the absence of unwanted carbide precipitates under these conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial carbon atoms occupying octahedral sites in the BCC lattice, which can locally relax lattice distortions and modify the bonding environment.
generation.mechanism: The added interstitial C is expected to counterbalance the high localized electronegativity differences (induced by Mo) by subtly altering the local electronic structure. This facilitates enhanced dislocation mobility (and may even promote the activation of additional deformation mechanisms such as localized twinning) while retaining the solid solution strengthening conferred by Mo, thus yielding a ductile yet strong microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the carbon-doped NbZrTiHfMo should exhibit a notable increase in compressive plastic strain (for instance, an improvement from very low ductility to a target increase of over 20% relative compressive strain) while the compressive yield strength remains within roughly 10% of 1719 MPa.
generation.baseline: The undoped equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, demonstrating very high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but minimal room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only for very low carbon contents (ideally below 1 at%) to avoid the formation of carbide precipitates which would otherwise deteriorate the ductility and possibly lower the yield strength. The improvement is specifically targeted at room-temperature compression behavior and might not extend to other loading regimes or elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: This proposition builds on findings from studies of interstitial-alloying in HEAs (e.g., the reported improvements in ductility via joint twinning and transformation-induced plasticity in systems with interstitial C as seen in PMC5227964) and the established role of high Mo content in increasing electronegativity differences and brittleness (PMC7514121). What is new here is applying a controlled interstitial doping strategy to the NbZrTiHfMo system to directly offset the Mo-induced brittleness. The precise quantitative extent of ductility improvement and the optimal carbon level remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloys under identical conditions, one set without and the other with ~0.5 at% added carbon. After identical homogenization treatments, conduct room-temperature compression tests and perform microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM and XRD) to check for carbide formation, lattice distortion levels, and dislocation behavior.
measurements: Yield strength and compressive plastic strain from stress–strain curves
Microstructural characterization to detect any precipitate (carbide) formation
Lattice parameter and local bonding environment analysis (e.g., via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) the carbon-doped alloy exhibits a significant drop in yield strength (greater than 10% reduction from 1719 MPa), or (b) no significant improvement in room-temperature compressive ductility is observed (i.e., less than a 10–20% relative increase compared to the baseline), or (c) undesired carbide phases are detected even at the low carbon concentration, indicating that interstitial C does not remain in solution.

cited_evidence.text: Our findings demonstrate a new alloy design concept of interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs. The excellent strength-ductility combination of these new materials has very large potential to break the inverse strength-ductility relationship. Also, owing to the unique combination of strengthening mechanisms invoked and the option for interstitial-driven tuning of phase (in)stability further optimization potential is at hand. Indeed, such a broad spectrum of deformation and strengthening mechanisms has never been realized in one single bulk material to date. Also, the interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA described here was synthesized by simple addition of interstitial carbon during well-established bulk metallurgical processes available worldwide in metallurgical industries, hence, such alloys can be readily realized in commercial operations.

Figure 2 shows the X-Ray diffraction patterns. The main phase of the Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy series is a BCC disordered solid solution. The asymmetry of (200) and (211) peaks are shown in the diffraction pattern results from the cored dendritic structure. The composition variation of dendritic and interdendritic areas causes a little difference in the lattice constant. The lattice constants of the Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy series listed in Table 2 are in the range of 3.305 to 3.400 Å calculated by the Nelson–Riley extrapolation function. Referring to the phase diagrams of each binary alloy between Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr, Hf-Mo, and Mo-Zr binary alloys form Mo2Hf and Mo2Zr, respectively, in a certain range of composition even at high temperature. However, these two intermetallic compounds or others do not show up in Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys, which means the high entropy effect has a significant benefit in forming simple BCC solid solution in this alloy system especially at high temperature.
